messages.subject: Fitting detection functions: Visually or AIC? / common(?) errors.
parts:
Hello, 

I am trying to fit a detection function to my data using the ds() function in R Studio. I have a few models that have been run through summarize_ds_models(): Half Normal (HN) key with (and without) observer and size as covariates, and the Hazard-Rate (HR) key with and without the same covariates. According to the summary funciton, the HR key with formula = ~obs+size fits best. The difference in AIC values between the models is HR with ~obs+size with best fit at 0 AIC, while HN with same covariates is best of the HN-models at around 150. 

However, looking at the plotted detection functions of both models, HN looks good, but the HR model seems very odd (see figures). The HR-model's histogram is very low, with an approx. 0.3 sightability at g(0), leading to an overestimate in my abundance call. With the HR plot looking odd but with the best fit, and HN looking best but with a worse fit - which one should I choose? 

Alternatively (and most likely the issue), what could be wrong with my HR detection function? 

I've seen a few errors regarding using unary operators, and convergence issues in some of my other models - does anyone have an explanation for what the root of these errors are? 

Figures:
all.hn.null.t - HN, no covariates, truncation = 15%
all.hr.null - HR, no covariates, no truncation
all.hr.obs.sz - HR, ~obs+size, no truncation
all.hr.obs.sz.t - HR, ~obs+size, truncation = 15%


Thanks, hope everyone is having a nice weekend!

Elling Johannessen

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: {Filename?} [distance-sampling] Fitting detection functions: Visually or AIC? / common(?) errors.
parts:
Elling, it’s not so much that the hazard-rate fit that is odd, it’s just trying to fit your data, and those data are odd.  You have a huge spike at or near zero.  You need to understand what causes that.  Are there problems with distance estimation?  Or are you getting perpendicular distances from radial distances plus angles, with many angles rounded to zero?  Or is detection probability extremely variable, with some animals only detectable very close to the line, and others detectable at large distances?  With these data, you certainly need to truncate, and you’ll probably need to truncate substantially more than 15% of your data, given how long the tail of the distribution is.

 

It's important to realise that in your analyses, g(0)=1 by assumption, so your statement of ‘approx 0.3 sightability at g(0)’ is incorrect.  But your data have such a sharp fall-off that the flexible hazard-rate model has to fall extremely rapidly from one to fit your data, while the half-normal model makes little attempt to fit the distances close to zero.  Unfortunately, with such data, reliable estimation is unlikely to be possible.  If the problem with your data is caused by failure of an assumption, then you need to address this for future surveys.  If you believe this is not the issue, try plotting the histogram with more intervals, especially having several intervals spanning the first 100 (m?) or so, to see the pattern of fall-off very close to the line.  It is not possible to advise on appropriate analysis here without much more detail about the study, and why the data are so problematic.

 

Steve Buckland

parts:
Steve, thank you for your input. And apologies for some of my formulations. Distance estimation should be fine, I'm using angular distances and angles to find perpendicular distances to the track line. 

A few thoughts I have are: 
1) low angles could potentially have been rounded to zero (as you mentioned) in some instances, but playing with the numbers (in a faux dataset) and changing angles from 0 up to 5 (the feasible margin of error), has no effect. 
2) There have also been large variations of 'sightability' during effort (visibility ranging from 300m to horizon) depending on various weather conditions (fog, wind, swell). I tried adding these factors to the formula, but still, it doesn't change the fact that distance=0 for such a (I'm assuming abnormally) large portion of the observations. 
3) Parts of the transect are through fields of icebergs, drastically reducing detection range in those momentary instances (because of their height). This also leads to a -- let's call it a frontal-transect-bias -- where the ship chooses the track which avoids ice, leading to higher detection rate on the track line. These observations were not many though. 
4) Ship movement. Parts of the transect were through geographically constrained areas such as straits, also potentially leading to a transect-bias.

This is not a traditional line-transect survey, but rather using platforms-of-opportunity. And these specific data reflect a rather geographically constrained stratum as well. So I think that might explain the situation. Based on these thoughts, could redrawing the strata shapefiles to exclude the more spatially limited areas be an idea? Or is this method not feasible at all in these circumstances?

Elling

messages.subject: RE: {Filename?} [distance-sampling] Fitting detection functions: Visually or AIC? / common(?) errors.
parts:
Elling, you don’t say what the study species is.  In addition to the issues you mention, could animals be attracted to the line, e.g. to ride the bow wave?  Yes, probably better to exclude narrow straits from your area when you try to estimate abundance.  Possibly any areas with a high density of icebergs too.  In both cases, you may have quite extreme departure from the assumption that animals are uniformly distributed with distance from the line.

 

In my experience, angles quite a lot larger than 5 deg can be rounded to zero.  If an animal is seen, observers tend to try to follow the animal.  By the time they record distance and angle, they may have lost the animal, and have only a vague idea of where it was.  Careful training, and a protocol for dealing with issues like this, can help.  Many years ago, when I first got involved in this type of survey, Antarctic minke whale surveys consistently showed a spike in the data like yours.  The problem was angles rounded to zero.  The next year, the message got through, so observers rounded instead to either 2 or 3 deg, and the problem was just as severe!  Angle boards were introduced in an effort to improve estimates, to no avail – the crew, who had lots of experience searching for whales on whaling vessels, didn’t consider they needed the boards.  So next time, the chief scientist overseeing the cruise took part in the distance and angle experiments that had been set up to try to resolve the problem.  He out-performed all of the experienced crew members, after which they used the angle boards, and the problem disappeared completely.  Your circumstances may be very different, but it is worth considering how the observers operate.

 

You say you have distance=0 for a large proportion of observations.  Look at how many of those have a radial distance of zero.  If a high proportion, then the problem is animals being attracted to the vessel.  In this case, you need observers to be detecting animals before they respond to the ship – which may be problematic.  If most of the zeros are a result of the angle being recorded as zero, then I suspect the error in angle estimates is substantially larger than you realise.

 

Sorry not to be more helpful.

 

Steve

Steve, this is a multi-species study, but in this stratum and these specific data the observations are mostly humpback whales (~95%) with the occasional fin and minke, grouped as krill-predators. As I experienced, fins and minke are shyer than humpbacks, but none of them were bow riding like the hourglass dolphins, for example, we recorded in a different stratum. I'll draw up new strata later today though. 

That's quite the anecdote! Theory was discussed on board, including the importance of g(0) = 1, so effort may have been subconsciously slightly higher on the trackline. However, I am sure of this for only one of the ships. The other ship also has this 'off' shape in its detection function, and also had the more experienced MMSO's. 

Angular distances vary from 100 meters to 3500 meters, but because the angle is 0 (or in reality, probably 0-5 degs), the perpendicular distance is 0, which will less accurate at larger distances as well. Is it an option to truncate outliers of the angular distances?  I highly doubt the errors in angle estimates exceed 5 degrees - leading me to hope that I find a better ddf from my new strata. 

Thanks for the insight, Steve, it's a complicated science for a Master student to get a solid understanding in a limited amount of time. I'm picking up your 'Advanced Distance Sampling' book at the library on Monday :)

Elling

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: {Filename?} [distance-sampling] Fitting detection functions: Visually or AIC? / common(?) errors.
parts:
Back in the 1980s, we developed ‘smearing’ to try to reduce the effect of rounding angles to zero.  It was never very successful, largely because a proportion of sightings appeared to be recorded as zero angle when the real angle was substantially larger.  My guess is that this occurred when there was a brief sighting that was not resighted, and the delay in recording an angle meant that the observer was unsure of the original location, and tended to record zero angle if it was somewhere ahead.  You can easily test your belief that zero angles were in reality no larger than 5.  Simulate some data with a reasonable pattern of search effort (simulating from a 2-dimensional hazard-rate model would be ideal), and see if you get as spiked a distribution as for your real data, if angles up to 5 are rounded to zero.  I would be very surprised if you do …

 

You might also want to look at whether the proportion of zero angles varies appreciably by observer – it’s quite possible that the accuracy of recording varies by observer.

 

When you have non-random transect lines, it may be worth considering fitting a density surface model, where it is less critical that lines are located independently of the animals.

 

Anyway, I hope you find a way to utilise your data fully.

Steve

søndag 14. juni 2020 10.27.22 UTC+2 skrev Stephen Buckland følgende:

Elling, you don’t say what the study species is.  In addition to the issues you mention, could animals be attracted to the line, e.g. to ride the bow wave?  Yes, probably better to exclude narrow straits from your area when you try to estimate abundance.  Possibly any areas with a high density of icebergs too.  In both cases, you may have quite extreme departure from the assumption that animals are uniformly distributed with distance from the line.

 

In my experience, angles quite a lot larger than 5 deg can be rounded to zero.  If an animal is seen, observers tend to try to follow the animal.  By the time they record distance and angle, they may have lost the animal, and have only a vague idea of where it was.  Careful training, and a protocol for dealing with issues like this, can help.  Many years ago, when I first got involved in this type of survey, Antarctic minke whale surveys consistently showed a spike in the data like yours.  The problem was angles rounded to zero.  The next year, the message got through, so observers rounded instead to either 2 or 3 deg, and the problem was just as severe!  Angle boards were introduced in an effort to improve estimates, to no avail – the crew, who had lots of experience searching for whales on whaling vessels, didn’t consider they needed the boards.  So next time, the chief scientist overseeing the cruise took part in the distance and angle experiments that had been set up to try to resolve the problem.  He out-performed all of the experienced crew members, after which they used the angle boards, and the problem disappeared completely.  Your circumstances may be very different, but it is worth considering how the observers operate.

 

You say you have distance=0 for a large proportion of observations.  Look at how many of those have a radial distance of zero.  If a high proportion, then the problem is animals being attracted to the vessel.  In this case, you need observers to be detecting animals before they respond to the ship – which may be problematic.  If most of the zeros are a result of the angle being recorded as zero, then I suspect the error in angle estimates is substantially larger than you realise.

 

Sorry not to be more helpful.

 

Steve

Elling, it’s not so much that the hazard-rate fit that is odd, it’s just trying to fit your data, and those data are odd.  You have a huge spike at or near zero.  You need to understand what causes that.  Are there problems with distance estimation?  Or are you getting perpendicular distances from radial distances plus angles, with many angles rounded to zero?  Or is detection probability extremely variable, with some animals only detectable very close to the line, and others detectable at large distances?  With these data, you certainly need to truncate, and you’ll probably need to truncate substantially more than 15% of your data, given how long the tail of the distribution is.

 

It's important to realise that in your analyses, g(0)=1 by assumption, so your statement of ‘approx 0.3 sightability at g(0)’ is incorrect.  But your data have such a sharp fall-off that the flexible hazard-rate model has to fall extremely rapidly from one to fit your data, while the half-normal model makes little attempt to fit the distances close to zero.  Unfortunately, with such data, reliable estimation is unlikely to be possible.  If the problem with your data is caused by failure of an assumption, then you need to address this for future surveys.  If you believe this is not the issue, try plotting the histogram with more intervals, especially having several intervals spanning the first 100 (m?) or so, to see the pattern of fall-off very close to the line.  It is not possible to advise on appropriate analysis here without much more detail about the study, and why the data are so problematic.

 

Steve Buckland
